task: Write one sentence of your own using the word derelict. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know derelict should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Past the fairgrounds the derelict drive-in rots in the weeds, its screen peeled to the boards and its speaker posts leaning forty different ways.
A neglected building still has an owner who ought to show up; derelict means the caring stopped altogether and the rot moved in.
Ruined goes past derelict: a derelict warehouse still stands to be photographed, while a ruined one has come down to rubble and sky.

Abandoned says only that the owners left — it tells you nothing about the state of what they left behind. A freshly locked cottage can be abandoned and still spotless. Derelict needs more: the place was abandoned and then rotted, the neglect written all over it.

Dilapidated judges condition alone — falling apart after years without upkeep — and says nothing about whether anyone is still there. A dilapidated bridge can carry traffic every day. Derelict makes both claims at once: no one uses the place anymore, and the decay has moved in behind them.

The plow blade in the museum case is a relic of the valley's first farm.
Derelict means abandoned and run-down.
Below Fourth Street there is a subway platform the trains pass without slowing.
Closed in 1945, it has sat derelict ever since: tiles furred with soot, a shuttered fare window with its glass still cranked half open, an advertisement for a hat store three owners dead.
Nobody maintains it; nobody even claims it.
Derelict is the right word because it needs both halves: abandoned and run-down.
A locked summer cottage is merely empty — someone still cares for it.
A shabby but crowded diner is merely worn.
The platform has lost both its people and its upkeep, and that double desertion is what derelict certifies.

Every spring, Alvarez walks the river ward with a clipboard, sorting the ward's failing buildings into columns for the housing office.
A boarded bakery whose owner still pays taxes goes in one column; a sagging rowhouse with a family inside goes in another.
The old glassworks is different.
No one has worked a shift there since 1987, its skylights have fallen through, and the last holding company dissolved decades ago.
Alvarez marks it derelict — the only word on her sheet, she says, that covers a building nobody uses, nobody owns, and weather is slowly taking apart.
Buildings in that column skip the repair fund entirely.
The city lists them for demolition or, when the bones are good, for full rebuilding as public housing.
